title: The Day the Law Was Read
sum: With the wall finished, the story turns from stones to a people. On the first day of the seventh month all the people gather in the square by the Water Gate, men and women and every child old enough to understand, and ask Ezra to bring out the scroll of Moses' law. He reads it from a wooden platform from first light until noon, while Levites move among the crowd explaining what was read. The people weep as they hear it. Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites stop them: the day is holy, a day for rich food and shared portions, "because the joy of the LORD is your stronghold" (8:10).

The next day the leaders come back to study, and they find the law of the Feast of Booths. The whole community goes out for branches and builds booths on roofs, in courtyards and in the squares, and keeps the feast for seven days with the law read every day. The narrator says Israel had not kept it this way since Joshua's time. The people of the wall have become a people of the book.
readings: Read as history

The reading fits what is known of the Persian period: a community organized around a written law, an assembly at a city gate rather than in the Temple, and Levites acting as teachers. Most historians accept that a public reading under Ezra lay behind the account, though they debate when it happened (see below). Its details, from the platform and the named men beside Ezra to the booths in named squares, read like the report of a witness.
Read as the book's turning point

Tamara Eskenazi and others read Ezra–Nehemiah as a story in which the house of God grows from a building into a people. Chapter 8 is where that happens: the scroll is opened before "all the people" (8:5), the people themselves call for it (8:1), and understanding, not only hearing, is stressed six times. The joy of 8:12 and 8:17 is the same joy that returns at the wall's dedication (12:43). Chapters 8–10 move from hearing (8) to confession (9) to commitment (10), the shape of covenant renewal.
Read as a model for worship

Jews have long seen here the pattern of synagogue reading: a scroll lifted before the congregation, the people standing, blessing and "Amen," reading from a raised platform, and explanation in the people's language (Bavli Megillah 3a). Christians have seen the pattern of preaching: the word read aloud and its meaning explained. Both traditions read the turn from tears to feasting as a lesson about how the law should be received.

views.H: A true account of the assembly of 445 BC (or, on another reading of the order, of 458 BC), with Ezra reading the law of Moses that he had brought from Babylon. The joint presence of Nehemiah and Ezra (8:9) shows the two leaders working together, as the book says.
views.C: Most critical scholars think chapter 8 comes from the Ezra story and once stood with Ezra 7–10: after Ezra 8 (so H. G. M. Williamson), or after Ezra 10, where 1 Esdras places it (1 Esdras 9:37–55). On this view an editor moved it here to crown the building of the wall with the hearing of the law, and many think Nehemiah's name in 8:9 was added then (see the variant note). What the "scroll of Moses' law" contained, the Pentateuch in something close to its present form or an earlier collection, is also debated.
views.A: Persian rulers backed local laws and temple customs across the empire, and Ezra came with the king's authority to teach "your God's law" (Ezra 7:25). A public reading of the law in Aramaic-speaking Judah fits the period's use of translation: Aramaic was the empire's official language, and many Judeans may have needed help with Hebrew (see the note on 8:8).
views.J: The rabbis read 8:8 as the origin of the Targum: "They read aloud" is the text, "explaining it" is translation, "they set out its meaning" is dividing the verses, and "the people grasped what was read" means the accents or the traditions of reading (Bavli Megillah 3a; Bavli Nedarim 37b). Ezra is credited with setting the Torah reading on Sabbath afternoons and fixing how many read, and how much, on Mondays and Thursdays (Bavli Bava Kamma 82a). The day of 8:2, the first of the seventh month, is Rosh Hashanah, and the command to eat rich food and send portions is cited for its festive meals.
views.X: Christian preachers have long taken 8:8 as the charter for expository preaching: read the text, explain it, and help people understand. Protestant traditions in particular have cited the scene of a whole people hearing Scripture explained in words they understood, both for preaching and for translating the Bible. "The joy of the LORD is your stronghold" (8:10) is one of the most quoted verses of the book in Christian devotion, read as a call to find strength in God's goodness rather than in grief for sin.

deep.b:
Chapter 8 tells of Ezra, in the third person, in the middle of Nehemiah's first-person memoir, which stops at 7:73 and resumes at 12:31. That is why its place has been debated.

Where it now stands. The traditional view, and that of many literary readers, is that the events happened in the seventh month of 445 BC, just after the wall was finished on the 25th of Elul (6:15). Ezra had been in Jerusalem since 458 BC teaching the law (Ezra 7:10), and the new safety of the city gave the occasion for a great public reading. Nehemiah's presence (8:9; 12:26) is taken at face value.

After Ezra 8. Some scholars, including Williamson, think the reading came in Ezra's first year, in the seventh month after his arrival in the fifth month (Ezra 7:8–9), and before the marriage crisis of Ezra 9–10. On this view the law was read first and then applied.

After Ezra 10. A minority follow 1 Esdras, which places the reading straight after the marriage reform (1 Esdras 9:37–55), and think that is the original order. 1 Esdras, though, ends with the people gathering and may be incomplete.

Those who date Ezra to 398 BC, after Nehemiah, also have to explain the joint scene of 8:9 (see the note on 12:26). The site's Ezra notes give the three views on where the chapter belongs (see the note on Ezra 9:1) and the arguments over Ezra's date (the Ezra 7 page). Wherever the events first stood, the book as it now reads joins them to the wall on purpose: the city is secured, then the people are formed by the law.

deep.h: 1 Esdras 9:37–55: the same day in Greek
deep.b:
1 Esdras, a Greek retelling of the end of Chronicles, Ezra and this chapter, gives a parallel account. It has no Nehemiah: in 9:49 "Attharates," a form of the Hebrew title tirshata "governor," speaks to Ezra, whom it calls "the high priest and reader." It dates the gathering to the new moon of the seventh month, gives the Levites' names in a different form (9:48), and has a different promise in place of 8:10: "for the Lord will glorify you" (9:52). It ends with the people going to feast because they had been taught the words, and then "they were gathered," the start of a sentence the book never finishes (9:55).

The Greek was checked here in Rahlfs' edition. It shows how the story of Ezra could be told without Nehemiah, which supports the critical view that the joint scene is the work of the editor of Ezra–Nehemiah. It does not prove it: 1 Esdras is selective throughout and leaves out all of Nehemiah's memoir, so it had no reason to keep him. The variant notes on 8:7, 8:9 and 8:10 set out the readings.

deep.title: Why did they weep?
deep.b: Claude's reading. The text says only that the people wept "as they listened to what the law said" (8:9). Most readers assume they were grieved by sin. But the day was the first of the seventh month, and the law they heard included Deuteronomy's promise that a scattered people would be gathered back to their land if they returned to the LORD (Deuteronomy 30:1–5). A people who had come back from exile, and had just closed their city's walls, may have wept also because they heard their own story told. This overlaps a view already given in the note on 8:9, that a scattered people was moved to hear its own story read aloud; what is added here is only the link to Deuteronomy 30:1–5 and the seventh-month setting. The leaders' answer fits either reason: on a holy day the right response to the law is to eat, share, and rejoice.

echoes: Deuteronomy 31:9–13; Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; Joshua 8:34–35; 2 Kings 23:1–3; Ezra 3:4; Ezra 7:10; 1 Esdras 9:37–55; Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:15

settings.by: Ezra the scribe, with thirteen Levites explaining
settings.to: All the people of Judah gathered in Jerusalem: men, women and children old enough to understand, standing in the square by the Water Gate
settings.when: The first day of the seventh month (Tishri), at a feast day, after the wall was finished in Elul (6:15)
settings.why: To make the whole community, not only priests and scribes, hear and understand the law that was to govern them. Deuteronomy had commanded that the law be read before all Israel, men, women, children and foreigners, at the Feast of Booths every seventh year (Deuteronomy 31:10–13). Here the people themselves ask for it. The Levites' explanations made the reading a lesson, not a ceremony: the stress falls on understanding.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers in Persian-period Judah, this was the founding scene of their life as a people of the law: the moment when the community gathered at the walls agreed to be ruled by Moses' Torah.
views: A real assembly under Ezra, in 445 BC if the book's order is followed, or in 458 BC if the chapter has been moved (see above).

Many scholars think the scene was shaped to match the reading of the law under Moses, Joshua and Josiah (Deuteronomy 31; Joshua 8:34–35; 2 Kings 23:1–3), so that the returned community could see itself as Israel renewed.

settings.what: "Today is holy": the leaders stop the weeping
settings.by: Nehemiah the governor, Ezra, and the Levites (as the Hebrew presents them)
settings.to: The weeping crowd at the Water Gate
settings.when: The same day, after the reading, at the time for the feast
settings.why: To turn grief into celebration. The leaders do not say the people's sorrow is wrong; they say the day is holy and must be kept as a feast. The command to send portions to "those who have nothing ready" makes the feast include the poor, as Deuteronomy's festival laws require (Deuteronomy 16:14).

settings.what: The Feast of Booths, found in the law
settings.by: The narrator; the proclamation of 8:15 by the leaders
settings.to: The heads of families, priests and Levites who came to study (8:13); then all the towns of Judah and Jerusalem (8:15)
settings.when: The second day of the seventh month, and the feast from the fifteenth to the twenty-second
settings.why: To show the law being put into practice at once. The leaders find the command in Leviticus 23:39–43, proclaim it, and the whole people build booths. The stress on "as it is written" (8:15) and on reading every day (8:18) shows a community learning to shape its year by the written law. The booths recalled the wilderness, when Israel lived in shelters after leaving Egypt (Leviticus 23:43), a fitting memory for people back from a second exodus.
settings.readers: Later readers learned from this how to keep Sukkot: branches from the hills, booths on roofs and in courtyards, and the reading of the law through the feast.

traditions.q: The Levites explained the law so that the people understood (Nehemiah 8:7–8). Who has the authority to explain Scripture?
views: The task of giving the true meaning of God's word, written or handed down, belongs to the living teaching office of the Church, the bishops with the pope; this office serves the word and is not above it (Dei Verbum 10). Catholics are urged to read the Bible in their own language within that faith.
Scripture lives inside the Church's Tradition and is read with the mind of the fathers and the liturgy. A private reading is tested against that shared mind, guarded by the bishops.

Scripture alone is the rule by which all teachers and teachings are judged (Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm). Yet no one should teach publicly in the church without a proper call (Augsburg Confession 14), as the Levites were appointed.

What must be known for salvation is so clear in Scripture that the learned and the unlearned can understand it by ordinary means, and the supreme judge in every dispute is the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture (Westminster Confession 1.7, 1.10). Preaching that reads and explains the text is God's main way of teaching his people.

Each believer is competent, under the Holy Spirit, to read and understand Scripture for himself, as E. Y. Mullins argued (The Axioms of Religion, 1908). Pastors teach, but no church body can bind a believer's conscience.

title: A Nation's Confession
sum: Two days after the feast ended, the mood changes. On the twenty-fourth of the month the Israelites gather fasting, in sackcloth, with soil on their heads. They separate from foreigners, read the law for a quarter of the day and confess for another quarter. Then the Levites lead the longest prayer in the Bible outside the Psalms.

The prayer retells Israel's whole story as a story of God's faithfulness and Israel's failure: creation, Abraham, the exodus, Sinai, the wilderness, the conquest, the judges, the prophets, and the handing over to foreign peoples. Again and again Israel rebels and God, "gracious and compassionate" (9:17, 9:31), does not desert them. It ends not with a request for freedom but with a description of the present: the people are slaves in their own land, its harvest going to foreign kings. Out of that distress they make a written, sealed agreement (9:38).
readings: Read as liturgy

The prayer is built from Scripture. It quotes or alludes to Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges and the Psalms, and its confession of God's character in 9:17 quotes Exodus 34:6. Mark Boda has shown how it weaves these traditions into a new prayer for the community. It belongs with the other great penitential prayers of the period (Ezra 9:6–15; Daniel 9:4–19) and may have been used in worship before it was placed here.
Read as a political statement

The prayer ends with an unusually sharp line: "Here we are today: slaves!" (9:36), and the land's produce goes "to the kings you have put over us for our sins" (9:37). It does not thank the Persian kings, as Ezra's prayer does (Ezra 9:9). Some scholars read it as a voice of discontent under imperial rule, kept beside Nehemiah's loyal service at court. Others read it as theology, not protest: the people accept foreign rule as the result of their sin and ask God to see their hardship.

views.H: The Levites led the people in this prayer in the seventh month of 445 BC. Its survey of history reflects Israel's understanding of its past as it is told in the Torah and the Former Prophets, and its confession is that of the people who had just heard the law.
views.C: Most critical scholars think the prayer was composed separately, perhaps earlier, and placed here by the editor. H. G. M. Williamson argued that its language and its silence about the exile in Babylon suggest it came from Judeans who had stayed in the land; others date it to the early Persian period or later. The Greek adds "And Ezra said" at 9:6, which the RSV and NRSV follow (see the variant note), but the Hebrew gives no author beyond the Levites.
views.A: "Slaves" in 9:36 describes subjects of the Persian empire paying tribute. Persian records show the burden of taxes paid in kind and in silver from the western provinces, which Nehemiah 5:4 also mentions. Persian kings claimed rights over subjects' bodies and cattle through levies and forced labor, as 9:37 complains.
views.J: 9:6–11 is recited every morning in the Jewish prayer service, from "It is you who are the LORD" through the crossing of the sea, as a bridge to the Song at the Sea (Exodus 15). The fast of 9:1 was a model for later fasts with confession. The rabbis read 9:4, "a great cry," as the prayer that the evil inclination for idolatry be taken away (Bavli Yoma 69b).
views.X: Christians have used Nehemiah 9 as a model of corporate confession: a community confessing not only its own sins but its ancestors', and owning the history of its people (9:2, 9:33–34). The prayer's survey of history is often compared with Stephen's speech in Acts 7, which also tells Israel's story as a story of repeated resistance. Its confession that God is "in the right" (9:8, 9:33) has been a pattern for prayers of confession in Christian worship.

deep.b:
Almost every line echoes an earlier text. Creation (9:6) recalls Genesis 1–2. Abraham's faithful heart and the covenant to give the land (9:7–8) recall Genesis 12, 15 and 17. The exodus (9:9–11) borrows from the Song at the Sea, where the pursuers go down "like a stone" and "in the mighty waters" (Exodus 15:5; Exodus 15:10). Sinai (9:13–14) joins Exodus 19–20 and the Sabbath. The wilderness (9:15–21) draws on Exodus 16–17, Numbers 14 and Deuteronomy 8:4. The conquest (9:22–25) quotes Deuteronomy 6:11: houses full of good things, wells cut in the rock. The judges (9:26–28) follow the cycle of Judges 2:11–19. 9:29 quotes Leviticus 18:5: "If a human being does them, he will live by them" (Leviticus 18:5).

The center of the prayer is 9:17, where Israel appoints a leader to return to Egypt (Numbers 14:4) and God answers with the words he spoke to Moses after the golden calf: gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love (Exodus 34:6). The prayer applies that confession to every later crisis (9:19, 9:27, 9:28, 9:31). Its argument is that the God who did not desert Israel in the wilderness will not desert them now.
deep.refs: Genesis 15:18–21; Exodus 15:5; Exodus 34:6–7; Leviticus 18:5; Numbers 14:4; Deuteronomy 6:10–11; Deuteronomy 8:4; Judges 2:11–19; Psalm 106:1–48; Acts 7:2–53

deep.h: Confession in the first person plural
deep.b: The prayer moves from "they" to "we." For most of its length it tells what "our ancestors" did (9:16). At 9:33 it says "we have done what is wicked," and by 9:36–37 the present generation is speaking of itself. This is how the prayers of the period work (Ezra 9:6–7; Daniel 9:5–8): the community owns its ancestors' sins and does not claim to be better than them. Jewish and Christian readers have both taken this as a model. It also raises a question that the prayer leaves open: why should a returned people still be suffering for the sins of the generation that went into exile? The prayer answers only by pointing to God's compassion and asking that the hardship "not seem small" in his sight (9:32).

echoes: Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:1–4; Deuteronomy 6:10–11; Deuteronomy 10:17; Judges 2:11–19; 1 Kings 8:46–51; Psalm 78:1–72; Psalm 105:1–45; Psalm 106:1–48; Ezra 9:6–15; Daniel 9:4–19; Acts 7:2–53

settings.what: The day of fasting and confession
settings.by: The narrator; the call to bless (9:5) by eight Levites
settings.to: The Israelites assembled in Jerusalem, who had kept themselves apart from foreigners
settings.when: The twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, two days after the closing assembly of Booths
settings.why: To bring the people from hearing the law to confessing their failure to keep it, before they bind themselves to it in writing (9:38). The separation from "everyone of foreign birth" (9:2) marks the community that will make the pledge; it is not said here to involve marriages.

settings.by: The Levites named in 9:4–5, leading the people (the Greek adds Ezra at 9:6)
settings.to: God, spoken aloud before the whole assembly, which joins in confessing
settings.when: On the fast day, after the reading and confession of 9:3
settings.why: To praise God for his faithfulness through the whole story of Israel, to confess the people's repeated rebellion, and to lay their present hardship under Persia before God. It does not ask for anything in so many words; its request is implied in "let none of the hardship ... seem small in your sight" (9:32). Knowing that a whole people spoke it, and not one leader, explains its "we" and its ending in a covenant they all sign.
settings.readers: For readers in Persian Judah, the prayer explained why they were still subjects in their own land and gave them words to say so before God, while holding on to his compassion.
views: The traditional view: the Levites spoke it on the fast of 9:1.
Many scholars, including Williamson and Boda, think it was composed separately, perhaps by Judeans who had not gone into exile, and set here by the editor.

title: The Signed Agreement
sum: The "firm agreement" of 9:38 is set out. Eighty-four names head it: Nehemiah the governor and Zedekiah, twenty-one priests, seventeen Levites and forty-four leaders of the people. Then everyone else, men, women and children old enough to understand, binds themselves with a curse and an oath to keep God's law.

The pledge spells out what that means in their situation: no marriages with the peoples of the land, no buying from traders on the Sabbath, the seventh year let go and debts cancelled, a yearly temple tax, a rota for the wood for the altar, and the first fruits, firstborn and tithes brought to the Temple. It ends with a line the next chapters will test: "We will not desert our God's house" (10:39).
readings: Read as a covenant document

The chapter has the form of a treaty or legal agreement: a preamble, a list of signatories, an oath with a curse, and particular terms. It stands in a line with the covenants of Sinai (Exodus 24:3–8), Joshua (Joshua 24:25), Josiah (2 Kings 23:3) and Ezra (Ezra 10:3), but it is the first that is written and sealed by the people's leaders.
Read as interpretation of the law

David Clines showed that most of the terms are not simply copied from the Torah but work out how to apply it: the law forbids work on the Sabbath, and the pledge adds that buying from foreigners counts; the law commands wood for the altar fire, and the pledge sets up a rota to supply it. On this reading chapter 10 is an early example of the kind of reasoning later Jewish law developed.

views.H: The agreement was made and sealed in 445 BC, after the fast of chapter 9, and its signatories are the leaders of that day. Chapter 13 shows Nehemiah enforcing its terms years later.
views.C: Many scholars note that the terms of chapter 10 match the abuses Nehemiah corrects in chapter 13, point by point: mixed marriages, Sabbath trade, the Levites' support, the wood offering and first fruits. Some therefore think the pledge was made after Nehemiah's second term, as its result, and placed here by the editor; others think chapter 13 shows the pledge being broken. The list of signers seems to draw on the lists of 7:6–73 and 12:1–26.
views.A: The third of a shekel (10:32) was a silver weight, not a coin; Persian-period Judah used silver by weight and later small coins stamped "Yehud." Temples across the Persian empire were funded by a mix of royal grants and local dues, and the pledge shows Judah taking on support that the king's grant (Ezra 7:20–24) may no longer have covered.
views.J: The rabbis saw the pledge as the founding of rules to protect the Torah. The yearly temple tax became the half-shekel (Exodus 30:13; Mishnah Shekalim 1:1), and the wood offering became a festival on set days (Mishnah Taanit 4:5). The ban on buying on the Sabbath from a non-Jew became settled law.
views.X: Christian readers have often taken chapter 10 as a model of covenant renewal: a community confessing its sin (chapter 9) and then binding itself in concrete, practical terms. Others have noted that the pledge's failure in chapter 13 shows the limits of a covenant made by human resolve.

deep.b:
The terms fall into two groups. Separation (10:30–31): no marriages with the peoples of the land, following Deuteronomy 7:3 and Exodus 34:16; no buying from them on the Sabbath or a holy day; the seventh year left fallow (Exodus 23:10–11) and debts released (Deuteronomy 15:1–2). The Temple (10:32–39): a third of a shekel a year for its regular offerings; wood by lot for the altar fire that must never go out (Leviticus 6:12–13); the first fruits of crops and trees (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:2); the firstborn of sons and animals (Exodus 13:2; Exodus 13:12–13); the first of the dough (Numbers 15:20); and the tithes, with a priest present when the Levites collected them and the tithe of the tithe brought to the Temple (Numbers 18:26).

The tithe arrangements are more detailed than any one law. They combine Numbers 18, where the tithe goes to the Levites, with Deuteronomy, where it is eaten at the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 14:22–29). The pledge shows a community that read all its laws together and worked out how they fit.
deep.refs: 10:30–39; Exodus 23:10–11; Exodus 30:11–16; Leviticus 6:12–13; Numbers 18:21–32; Deuteronomy 7:3; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 15:1–2

echoes: Exodus 24:3–8; Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3; Deuteronomy 15:1–2; Joshua 24:25; 2 Kings 23:3; Ezra 10:3; Nehemiah 13:10–31; Malachi 3:8–10

settings.to: The assembly of chapter 9. The sealed document, with the names of the governor, the priestly houses, the Levites and the heads of the people's houses, was a record for the Temple archive and the community, like the sealed deeds of Jeremiah 32:10–14.
settings.when: After the fast of 9:1, as the agreement of 9:38 is sealed
settings.why: To show that the whole leadership, the governor, the priestly houses, the Levites and the heads of the people's families, put their names to the pledge. Many of the names are those of clans and houses rather than individuals, so the list commits whole families.

settings.what: The oath of the whole people
settings.by: The narrator, then the people as "we"
settings.to: God, before the assembly. It binds "the rest of the people": priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants and those who had kept apart for God's law, with their wives, sons and daughters old enough to understand
settings.when: At the sealing of the agreement
settings.why: To add the oath of every household to the seals of the leaders, under a curse on any who break it (compare Deuteronomy 29:12). The clauses that follow spell out what the oath means.

settings.to: Fathers of families, who arranged marriages: they will not give their daughters to the peoples of the land or take those peoples' daughters for their sons
settings.when: For all future marriages in Judah
settings.why: It applies Deuteronomy 7:3 (and Exodus 34:16) to the returned community among its neighbors. It names future marriages only and says nothing of existing ones. Many link it to the marriages Nehemiah finds in 13:23–27; whether it came before them or answers them is debated (see below).

settings.what: No buying on the Sabbath; the seventh year and debts
settings.to: Judean buyers, not the foreign sellers, who are not bound by Israel's law; and in the second half, landholders and creditors
settings.when: Every Sabbath and holy day; every seventh year
settings.why: The first half extends the Sabbath law (Exodus 20:10) to trade, in the spirit of Amos 8:5: Judeans will not buy what foreigners bring. Only in 13:19–21 does Nehemiah go further and keep the sellers out by shutting the gates. The second half joins the fallow year of Exodus 23:11 to the release of loans in Deuteronomy 15:2, and so answers the debt crisis of chapter 5.

settings.what: The yearly third of a shekel
settings.to: The pledgers themselves ("we put on ourselves"): every household of the community
settings.when: Each year
settings.why: To pay for the Temple's regular worship: the bread set in rows, the daily offerings, the Sabbaths, new moons and feasts, and the sin offerings. It is modeled on the half-shekel of Exodus 30:13, at a lower rate. It suggests that the Persian grants (Ezra 6:9–10; Ezra 7:20–22) were no longer enough, or no longer paid.

settings.to: The priests, Levites and people, by ancestral houses, each house in turn at its set time
settings.when: At set times year by year
settings.why: Leviticus 6:12–13 says the altar fire must never go out but does not say who supplies the wood. The lot shares the duty fairly among the families.

settings.what: First fruits, firstborn and the first of the dough
settings.to: Farming and herding households; the gifts go to the priests at the Temple
settings.when: Each year at harvest, and at each birth of a firstborn
settings.why: To keep the laws of first fruits (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:2), the firstborn (Exodus 13:2; Exodus 13:12–13; Numbers 18:15) and the first of the dough (Numbers 15:20–21), so that the priests are supported.

settings.to: Farmers, who give the tithe to the Levites in their towns; the Levites, who must collect with a priest present and carry a tenth of the tithe up to the Temple storerooms
settings.when: Each year
settings.why: To apply Numbers 18:21–26, where the tithe belongs to the Levites and a tenth of it to the priests, and to make the Temple storerooms the center of the system. The last line, "We will not desert our God's house," sums up the Temple clauses. Many read 13:10–13 as this clause failing; some think chapter 10 was drawn up afterward, from Nehemiah's reforms.
views: The traditional order: the pledge was made at the time of chapters 8–9 and later broken.
Some scholars think it records the settlement Nehemiah reached in his second term (chapter 13).

title: Filling the City
sum: The city had walls but few people (7:4). Now the leaders settle in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots so that one family in ten moves in. Those who volunteer are blessed. The chapter lists who lived there: men of Judah and Benjamin, priests, Levites, gatekeepers and their officers, with the numbers of each family.

The second half lists the towns where the rest of the people lived, from Beersheba in the south to Bethel and the coastal plain at Lod and Ono. The list goes further than the Persian province probably reached and may describe the ideal territory of Judah and Benjamin as much as the actual settlement.
readings: Read as administration

The chapter continues 7:4–5, where Nehemiah found the city empty and gathered the people to be registered. It is a record of a policy: repopulating a capital by lot and by volunteers. The list of residents is closely related to 1 Chronicles 9:2–34, which gives a similar list with different details, and the two may come from a common source.
Read as the holy city restored

Jerusalem is twice called "the holy city" (11:1, 11:18), a title Isaiah also uses (Isaiah 48:2; Isaiah 52:1). The tithe of people for the city echoes the tithe of produce for the Temple. The town list echoes Joshua 15 and 18, as if the land were being shared out again.

views.H: A true record of the resettlement of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day. The numbers (about 3,000 men in Jerusalem) fit a small capital of a small province.
views.C: Most scholars think the residents' list comes from an archive and was placed here to complete 7:4–5. Its relation to 1 Chronicles 9 is debated: one may depend on the other, or both on an older list. The town list (11:25–35) includes places such as Beersheba, Lachish and Ziklag that were probably outside the province of Yehud, which leads many to read it as an ideal picture drawn from Joshua.
views.A: Archaeological surveys, especially by Charles Carter and Oded Lipschits, suggest that Persian-period Jerusalem was small, perhaps a few hundred to 1,500 people, and that the province was thinly settled. Lachish had a Persian administrative building, and Persian-period remains appear at several of the southern towns, though the area was largely outside Yehud.
views.J: The rabbis counted volunteering to live in Jerusalem as a merit, and Jewish law later gave special honor to living in the Land of Israel and in Jerusalem. "The holy city" became a standard Jewish name for Jerusalem.
views.X: Christians have read the volunteers of 11:2 as an example of those who give up comfort for the sake of God's city. "The holy city" passes into the New Testament for Jerusalem (Matthew 4:5) and for the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:2).

echoes: 7:4–5; 1 Chronicles 9:2–34; Joshua 15:20–63; Joshua 18:21–28; Isaiah 52:1; Matthew 4:5; Revelation 21:2

settings.to: The people of Judah and Benjamin living in their towns
settings.when: After the wall was finished and the people registered (7:4–5)
settings.why: To give the walled city enough people to defend and run it. The lot spread the burden fairly, and the blessing on volunteers (11:2) shows that moving to the city was a sacrifice: it meant leaving land and kin.

settings.by: The narrator, from an archive list
settings.to: The community, and later generations who traced their families
settings.when: Nehemiah's time; the list may have been updated later
settings.why: To record the families who made up Jerusalem, and to show that the city held lay leaders, priests, Levites and gatekeepers in their proper places. For families in later centuries, being listed here proved their standing.

settings.what: The king's order for the singers
settings.to: The singers and those responsible for their daily share
settings.when: Nehemiah's time
settings.why: To note that the singers' daily support rested on a standing order, which explains their special place in the list.
views: Most think "the king" is Artaxerxes, as "the king's hand" in 11:24 suggests, perhaps continuing the tax exemption of Ezra 7:24.
Others read it as David's ordering of the singers (12:24; 1 Chronicles 25), recalled as a royal command.

settings.what: The towns of Judah and Benjamin
settings.to: The community of Yehud
settings.when: Nehemiah's time, or later
settings.why: To show the people settled across the land, from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom (11:30) and in Benjamin's towns. Whether it describes where people actually lived or the land as it ought to be is debated.
views: Some think it records Judean villages, including those outside the province's border.
Others think it was drawn from Joshua 15 and 18 to express the hope of the whole land.

title: Joy Heard Far Away
sum: The chapter opens with lists of priests and Levites, reaching from the first return under Zerubbabel and Jeshua in 538 BC through the generation of Joiakim to the high priest Jaddua, perhaps a century later. These lists anchor the community's leaders in an unbroken line.

Then Nehemiah's own voice returns for the dedication of the wall. Levites and singers are gathered from their villages; priests, people, gates and wall are purified; and two great choirs walk the top of the wall in opposite directions, with trumpets, lyres and harps, to meet in the Temple. Great sacrifices are offered, and "Jerusalem's gladness could be heard from far off" (12:43). The chapter ends with officials appointed over the storerooms and a picture of an ideal community supporting its Temple.
readings: Read as history

The lists come from Temple archives and the account of the dedication from Nehemiah's memoir. The procession route can be traced along the gates of chapter 3. The high priestly line reaches beyond Nehemiah's day, so the lists were updated after him (see the note on 12:10).
Read as the climax of the book

Ezra–Nehemiah builds toward this day. The Temple was dedicated with joy (Ezra 6:16), and now the city that holds it is dedicated with joy. The joy that was mixed with weeping at the founding of the Temple (Ezra 3:12–13) is now unmixed. Eskenazi and others read the procession as the whole community, leaders, priests and people, together claiming the city as holy.

views.H: The dedication followed soon after the wall was finished in 445 BC, and Ezra and Nehemiah led the two choirs together. The priestly and Levitical lists record the families who served from the first return to the writer's day.
views.C: Many scholars think the dedication account (12:27–43) originally followed 6:15 or 7:3 in Nehemiah's memoir and that chapters 8–11 were placed in between by the editor. Ezra's name in 12:36 and the joint mention in 12:26 are often thought to be editorial (see the notes). The list of high priests to Jaddua and "Darius the Persian" (12:22) suggest updating into the late Persian or early Greek period.
views.A: The Elephantine letter of 407 BC names the high priest Johanan (12:22–23), giving one fixed point for the list. Josephus' account of Jaddua meeting Alexander the Great in 332 BC (Jewish Antiquities 11.302–347) is legend in part but may preserve the right era for him. "Darius the Persian" may be Darius II (423–404 BC) or Darius III (336–330 BC).
views.J: The dedication (chanukkah) of the wall became a model for later dedications. Mishnah Shevuot 2:2 describes the rite for enlarging the city or the Temple courts: with the king, a prophet, the Urim and Thummim, the Sanhedrin, two thanksgiving offerings and song, a ritual clearly drawn from this chapter. The festival of Hanukkah later took its name from the same word.
views.X: Christians have read the two choirs meeting in the Temple as a picture of worship that unites God's people, and the joy heard far off as the witness of a worshiping community to those outside.

deep.b:
Nehemiah sets up two "thanksgiving choirs" (todot), each with a procession. The first, led by Hoshaiah with half of Judah's leaders, priests with trumpets, and the Levite Zechariah and his brothers with David's instruments, goes along the wall toward the Dung Gate, past the Spring Gate, and up the steps of the City of David to the Water Gate (12:31–37). Ezra walks at its head (12:36). The second, with Nehemiah and the other half of the people, goes the other way past the Tower of the Ovens, the Broad Wall, the Gate of Ephraim and the north towers to the Sheep Gate (12:38–39). Both meet in the Temple, where more priests with trumpets and singers led by Jezrahiah join them (12:40–42).

The order of the procession places the people's leaders, priests and Levites side by side, and puts the governor at the rear of his choir. The walk on the wall is a public claim that the city is restored, under God's protection, and holy. Psalm 48 invites a similar walk around Zion to count its towers.

echoes: Ezra 3:10–13; Ezra 6:16–22; 1 Chronicles 15:16–28; 2 Chronicles 5:12–14; 2 Chronicles 29:25–30; Psalm 48:12–14; Psalm 147:2; Isaiah 35:10; John 10:22

settings.what: The lists of priests and Levites
settings.by: The narrator, drawing on Temple records (12:23)
settings.to: The community of the Second Temple, whose priests and Levites traced their right to serve
settings.when: Compiled over generations, from the first return (538 BC) to the days of Jaddua
settings.why: To show unbroken succession: the priestly houses of Jeshua's day continued under Joiakim, and the Levites served by David's order. In a community where the right to serve depended on descent (Ezra 2:61–63), such lists settled who belonged. The parallel lists of 12:1–7 and 12:12–21 match house for house.

settings.to: The Levites and singers living in villages around Jerusalem
settings.when: Before the dedication of the wall
settings.why: To gather the Temple's musicians and to purify priests, people, gates and wall, so that the dedication would be holy. The purifying of the wall shows the city treated as holy ground.

settings.to: Inside the story, the whole community of Judah taking part; the account is written for God and for later readers
settings.when: 445 BC, soon after the wall was finished, or later in Nehemiah's first term
settings.why: To give thanks to God for the wall and to claim the city as his. Nehemiah tells it with himself in the second choir and the people's leaders in the first, showing a community united in worship. The note that the joy was heard far away answers the mockery of the neighbors (4:1–3): the city they laughed at is now singing.
settings.readers: For later readers, this was the day the city's restoration was complete, and the model for what a holy city should sound like.
views: Many scholars think it once followed 6:15 or 7:3.
The present order places it after the city was repopulated (11:1–2).

settings.to: The community of Judah
settings.when: "That same day" and in the time following
settings.why: To show the covenant of 10:35–39 working as it should: officials appointed, gifts gathered, priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers supported. The ideal sets up the next chapter, where it has broken down.

title: Remember Me
sum: The book ends not with the joy of the dedication but with a governor fighting to hold a community to its promises. When the law against Ammonites and Moabites is read, the people separate the "mixed crowd" from Israel. Then Nehemiah tells what he found when he came back from the Persian court after twelve years as governor: the priest Eliashib had given Tobiah the Ammonite a room in the Temple, the Levites had gone back to their fields for lack of tithes, the Sabbath was a market day, and men had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab whose children could not speak Hebrew.

He throws Tobiah's furniture out, restores the tithes and appoints trustworthy treasurers, shuts the city gates for the Sabbath, and confronts the men who married foreign wives, cursing and beating some and making them swear an oath. He drives away a grandson of the high priest who had married Sanballat's daughter. Between the reforms come his short prayers, and the book ends with the last: "My God, remember me for good" (13:31).
readings: Read as the covenant tested

Each reform answers a promise of chapter 10: the Temple storerooms and tithes (10:37–39), the Sabbath (10:31) and marriages (10:30). The covenant ended "We will not desert our God's house" (10:39); Nehemiah asks, "Why is God's house deserted?" (13:11). The book closes with the honest admission that renewed promises do not keep themselves.
Read as a memoir

Chapter 13 is Nehemiah's own account, and it shows his character more sharply than any other part of the book: decisive, courageous, quick to anger and conscious of his own record before God. The refrain "remember me" (13:14, 13:22, 13:31) makes the memoir a kind of report to God, as well as to readers.
Read as a debate about identity

Many modern readers find the chapter's treatment of foreigners troubling, and set it beside Ruth, Jonah and Isaiah 56, where foreigners are welcomed. Others read it in its setting: a small community, under foreign rule, losing its language and its Temple's support, that needed firm boundaries to survive. Both readings are argued below.

views.H: Nehemiah's own account of his second term, after 433/432 BC. The reforms were real, and they preserved the community's identity: its Temple, its Sabbath and its language.
views.C: Most scholars accept the chapter as part of Nehemiah's memoir, with 13:1–3 added by the editor to link it to the preceding chapters. They note that the reforms correspond to the terms of chapter 10 and debate which came first (see the chapter 10 page). Nehemiah's methods, especially the physical punishment in 13:25, are seen as those of a Persian governor with royal authority.
views.A: An Elephantine letter of 407 BC mentions the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, showing that the family still ruled there a generation later. The Tobiad family of Ammon remained powerful into the Greek period. Tyrian merchants and fish trade are attested in the Persian Levant, and Ashdod was the center of a coastal province.
views.J: The rabbis honored Nehemiah as a builder and reformer. But the Talmud faults him for self-regard: "Why was the book not called by his name? Because he took credit for himself" (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b, in summary), and because he spoke ill of the governors before him (5:15). The rabbis also read Deuteronomy 23:3 as applying to Moabite men only, so that Ruth's line was not excluded (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3).
views.X: Christian readers have admired Nehemiah's zeal for God's house and often compared his clearing of the Temple room with Jesus clearing the Temple (John 2:13–17). Many have also noted that the New Testament welcomes foreigners into God's people (Ephesians 2:11–22) and that Paul's guidance on mixed marriages is different: a believer should not leave an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). Some read 13:31 as a moving prayer of dependence, others as a sign of the limits of reform by law.

deep.b:
The chapter contains two actions against foreigners: the separation of the "mixed crowd" after the reading of Deuteronomy 23 (13:1–3), and Nehemiah's confrontation with men married to foreign women (13:23–28). Readers have judged them in very different ways.

Protection of a fragile community. Defenders, including Derek Kidner and H. G. M. Williamson, stress the setting. The returned community was a province of perhaps twenty or thirty thousand people, with a capital of a few thousand at most, surrounded by stronger neighbors whose leaders opposed them (chapters 4 and 6) and who had moved into the Temple itself (13:4–9). Children who could not speak Judean (13:24) could not take part in the reading of the law. Nehemiah's concern is religious, not racial: he cites Solomon, whose wives led him to other gods (13:26). And compared with Ezra's reform, his is restrained: he forbids future marriages by oath but, as told, breaks up no existing family, and he drives away only the priest whose marriage tied the high priest's house to Sanballat (13:28).

Harsh exclusion. Critics, including David Janzen, Harold Washington and Daniel Smith-Christopher, see an elite drawing ethnic lines to secure its own power, with women and children bearing the cost. They note that Nehemiah beats people and pulls out their hair (13:25), that "the mixed crowd" (13:3) is a wider group than the law named, and that other parts of the Bible welcome foreigners who join the people: Ruth the Moabite, the ancestor of David; the foreigners of Isaiah 56:3–7 who keep the Sabbath; Rahab. Katherine Southwood reads the reforms as the identity politics of returnees who did not recognize those who had stayed.

Many readers hold parts of both views: the reforms answered a real danger, and they also show the costs of drawing boundaries by force. The topic page on foreigners sets out how the Bible as a whole handles the question, and the notes on Ezra 9–10 discuss Ezra's reform.
deep.refs: 13:1–3; 13:23–28; Ezra 9:1–2; Ezra 10:3; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Ruth 1:16; Ruth 4:13–17; Isaiah 56:3–7

deep.b:
The Talmud asks why the book was not called by Nehemiah's name, since it is his memoir, and answers: because he took credit for himself, as in "My God, remember me for good" (5:19), and because he spoke badly of the governors before him (5:15), including Daniel, according to the Talmud (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). In the Talmud's tradition Ezra–Nehemiah is one book, called Ezra (Bava Batra 15a).

Others have read the prayers differently. Nehemiah does not ask people to remember him; he asks God. Similar prayers appear in inscriptions of officials of the time, such as Udjahorresnet in Egypt, who asked his gods to remember his good works, so the form was a common one. And 13:22 asks for pity "as your great loyal love allows," which places his hope in God's character rather than his own merit.

deep.title: A book that ends unfinished
deep.b: Claude's reading, which overlaps much published work: commentators on the book's ending, and David Clines on the Nehemiah memoir, read 13:4–31 as showing that the reforms do not hold. What is offered here is only the link to the open ending of Malachi. Ezra–Nehemiah could have ended at 12:43, with the joy heard far away. Instead it ends with broken promises, an angry governor, and a prayer. The placement may be deliberate: the book refuses to let its readers think that walls, lists and covenants complete the restoration. The last word is a request to God, not a report of success, and that leaves the story open in the way the prophets left it open (Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6), waiting for God to act.

echoes: Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Numbers 22:1–24:25; 1 Kings 11:1–8; Jeremiah 17:19–27; Numbers 25:10–13; Malachi 2:4–9; Malachi 3:8–10; Ezra 9:1–10:44; Ruth 1:16; Isaiah 56:3–7; John 2:13–17

settings.what: The reading of Deuteronomy 23 and the separation
settings.to: The people of Judah at a public reading of the law
settings.when: "That day": the editor links it to the dedication of 12:43, though it may belong to Nehemiah's second term
settings.why: To apply the law against Ammonites and Moabites entering "the assembly of God" (Deuteronomy 23:3–5). It introduces the Tobiah episode, since Tobiah was an Ammonite. What the separation involved, exclusion from worship, from full membership or from the land, is not said.
views: Many think "the assembly" meant the gathering for worship, from which those of foreign descent were now excluded.
A rule for membership and marriage
Others, following later Jewish law, read it as about marriage and full membership.

settings.to: Inside the story, Eliashib and the Temple staff; the account is written for God and readers
settings.when: On his return after 433/432 BC
settings.why: To show the Temple defiled by the presence of an Ammonite official, Nehemiah's old opponent (2:10), with the help of a priest. Clearing it and restoring the offerings protects the house that the covenant had promised not to desert (10:39).

settings.to: The officials of Judah, whom he confronts; the Levites and singers, whom he brings back
settings.when: On his return
settings.why: To restore the support of the Temple staff that the covenant had promised (10:37–39). Appointing four trustworthy men from different groups addresses the cause: the stores had been managed by a priest close to Tobiah. The prayer of 13:14 offers this work to God.

settings.to: The nobles of Judah (13:17); the traders camped outside the walls (13:21); the Levites he appoints (13:22)
settings.when: "In those days," during his second term
settings.why: To stop the Sabbath becoming a market day. The rule binds every Judean, and the gate closing binds foreign traders too, who had no Sabbath law of their own but could not sell in the city on that day. Nehemiah's argument (13:18) is drawn from Jeremiah 17: the city fell because its people broke the Sabbath. Nehemiah ends the section with a prayer (13:22), asking God to remember this too and to have pity on him by his great loyal love.

settings.to: Jewish men who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab
settings.when: "In those days," during his second term
settings.why: To stop further marriages that, in his view, were costing the community its language and its faith. He makes the men swear for their children and themselves. Unlike Ezra (Ezra 10:3), he does not, as told, require existing marriages to be ended. His argument from Solomon (13:26) makes the danger religious: foreign wives led even the wisest king into idolatry.
views: A small community losing its language and identity needed firm limits.
Women and children paid the price of a boundary drawn by men in power.

settings.what: The priest driven out and the last prayers
settings.to: The priest married to Sanballat's daughter; and God, in the prayers
settings.when: During his second term; the text gives no date
settings.why: To protect the high priestly family from a marriage that tied it to the governor of Samaria; Leviticus 21:14 requires the high priest to marry within his own people, and Nehemiah applies that to the high priest's house. Then 13:30–31 binds the priests and Levites to their duties, "each man at his own work," and the people to bring the wood offering at its set times and the first fruits, as pledged in 10:34–37. The prayers of 13:29 and 13:31 hand judgment and reward to God.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, this ending left them with the reforms to keep and with Nehemiah's prayer as their own: that God would remember them for good.

traditions.q: Nehemiah shut Jerusalem's gates to stop trade on the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:15–22). Does this bind Christians, and on which day?
views: The seventh day, Saturday, is still the Sabbath, a gift from creation kept in the Ten Commandments (Fundamental Beliefs 20). Nehemiah's stand against buying and selling on the Sabbath is a model for Christians today.

Since Christ rose, the Sabbath has moved to the first day, the Lord's Day, the Christian Sabbath. It is kept holy by resting from work, business and even recreation, and giving the day to worship and mercy; the Westminster Confession cites Nehemiah 13 for this (21.7–8). Scottish and Puritan laws long closed shops on Sunday.

Sunday, the day of the resurrection, fulfills the Sabbath. Catholics are to avoid work and business that keep them from worship and rest, and the Church asks that Sunday be protected as a legal day of rest (Catechism 2184–2188).

The Sabbath law of Moses no longer binds; the church keeps Sunday for good order and to hear God's word, not because the day itself is required (Augsburg Confession 28). Luther taught that the commandment means holding preaching and God's word sacred (Large Catechism).
